pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Seafood, Ready-to-Heat

content.title: About
content.content: This ready‑to‑heat meal consists of whole‑grain pasta topped with a tomato‑based sauce and a mix of seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid). The dish is fully cooked and only needs reheating in a microwave or on the stove. The combination of whole grains, tomatoes and seafood provides a balanced mix of protein, complex carbs and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta contains more fiber and micronutrients than traditional white‑flour pasta.
The tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Seafood is an excellent source of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for brain function.
The meal is designed for quick preparation: just 2‑3 minutes in the microwave.
No artificial preservatives or flavorings are added.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta helps regulate digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Quality protein source
items.content: Seafood provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, which helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood delivers EPA and DHA, supporting heart and brain health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta raises blood sugar more slowly than regular pasta.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: The product contains shrimp, mussels and squid, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce can be salty; individuals monitoring sodium intake should consider this.

items.title: Heat distribution
items.content: When microwaving, stir the dish to avoid hot spots and uneven heating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in the microwave for 2‑3 minutes or on the stovetop, stirring halfway through. Serve immediately; optional toppings include fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C. After thawing in the refrigerator, consume within 24 hours. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork is the meat of domesticated pigs and is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. Depending on the cut, the meat can be tender and juicy (e.g., tenderloin) or more robust and flavorful (e.g., shoulder). Pork is used in countless dishes: it can be grilled, roasted, braised, boiled, fried, or processed into sausages and cured products.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork accounts for about 36 % of global meat consumption.
Traditional dishes such as roast pork, schnitzel, pork stew, and dumplings feature pork in many cultures.
Pork is a rich source of vitamin B12, essential for red blood cell formation.
Pigs have an acute sense of smell—up to ten times more sensitive than humans.
In some religions (e.g., Islam and Judaism) pork consumption is prohibited.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork provides complete protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: Pork supplies zinc, selenium, and iron, which help immune function and cellular health.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: The meat contains creatine, beneficial for high‑intensity athletic performance.

items.title: Unsaturated fats in lean cuts
items.content: Lean pork cuts (e.g., tenderloin) provide beneficial polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Some pork cuts (such as bacon) are high in saturated fat, which can raise cholesterol when consumed in excess.

items.title: Parasites and bacteria
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor Trichinella or Salmonella; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Allergy or intolerance
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Sausages and ham often contain high levels of salt and preservatives, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pork can be grilled, roasted, braised, boiled, fried, or ground for burgers and sausages. Marinating in herbs, garlic, and an acid (lemon juice or vinegar) enhances tenderness and flavor. Lean cuts are best prepared with minimal added fat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh pork should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Frozen pork can be stored up to 6 months at –18 °C. Before cooking, check for off‑odors, gray discoloration, or a slimy surface, which indicate spoilage.
